targets.review_note: All dimensions below a reached maximum are freely accessible and their curses are suppressed. Add zero-cost downward edges and charge a magic upward destination curse. A minimum path never needs a paid jump below a previously reached maximum: it can skip that detour using free descent. Thus ordinary nonnegative Dijkstra captures the optimal increasing-maximum sequence without storing a visited-curse set.

targets.review_note: At each x, irrigated-and-fertilized cells form a vertical interval from the prefix minimum sprinkler y to the suffix maximum y. Both bounds are nonincreasing. A rectangle spanning columns a..b therefore has available height U[b]-L[a]+1, yielding h(h+1)/2 vertical intervals when positive. Three Fenwick moments of prior L values sum this quadratic for all b in O(N log N).

targets.review_note: Factor the odd modulus and count roots modulo each prime power, multiplying by CRT. For nonzero B, its p-adic valuation must be divisible by A. Removing this valuation leaves an equation in the cyclic unit group, with gcd(A,phi) roots iff B^(phi/gcd)=1. Account for free lifts by p^(valuation-rootvaluation). If B vanishes modulo the prime power, count roots whose valuation is at least ceil(e/A).

targets.review_note: Each odd-index chain is a finite coin-turning game; a coin at i has Grundy floor(log2(n/i)), and moving onto an occupied box removes both by XOR cancellation. XORing all initial coins telescopes to a bit checksum: bit d of n contributes d xor(d-1), with bit0 contributing0. Count zero-checksum binary numbers using digit DP, then unrank the kth positive one, explicitly skipping n=0.

targets.review_note: Bottom-up tree DP records whether the parent holds B, the current device(none/A/B), and whether any child holds B. An edge u-v is guarded by A/B at either endpoint or B adjacent to either endpoint. The child-B flag therefore covers every incident edge of u, while only B at u affects the next level. Combine children with an OR state enforcing that flag, and test every edge using these exact local conditions.

targets.review_note: The jth sweet of type i is a unit job released at floor((j-1)S/a_i)+1 and due at ceil(jS/a_i), obtained from both strict balance inequalities. Earliest-deadline-first among released jobs maximizes the feasible prefix. Multiple jobs due today make the current purchase impossible without breaking balance. Reaching the next multiple of S fixes every count exactly and returns to the same periodic quota state, from which a balanced unit-job schedule repeats forever.
